b: Birmingham, AL – Great fishing companies don’t simply build better tackle. They change the way anglers think. For the past 60 years, Daiwa has done exactly that.

Since opening its U.S. operation in California in 1966, the Japanese manufacturer has grown from an emerging overseas brand into one of the most influential names in bass fishing. Along the way, Daiwa has introduced technologies that have become industry standards, challenged conventional thinking about rods and reels and helped usher bass anglers into entirely new eras of fishing.

The company’s story began a decade earlier, when its first spinning reel rolled off the assembly line in 1955. Only a few years later, Daiwa began developing products specifically for the American market, recognizing that U.S. anglers demanded longer casts, heavier lines and equipment capable of handling larger fish. In September 1966, Daiwa Corporation officially opened its U.S. headquarters in Culver City, Calif., beginning what has become a six-decade relationship with American anglers.
From the beginning, innovation became the company’s calling card.

1970: Changing the Way Reels Were Built

During the 1970s, Daiwa established itself as a leader in spinning reel technology by embracing the skirted spool design, helping improve casting performance and line management at a time when spinning tackle was rapidly gaining popularity with bass anglers. It was one of several developments that transformed Daiwa from an upstart manufacturer into what many anglers simply referred to as “the reel company.”
But the company’s willingness to rethink conventional design didn’t stop there.

In 1979, Daiwa became the first manufacturer to build reel bodies and rotors from carbon graphite, reducing weight without sacrificing strength. At a time when aluminum was considered the obvious choice, Daiwa proved lighter materials could also deliver durability — a philosophy that continues to influence modern tackle design.

Throughout its history, Daiwa has focused on engineering first. The company pioneered magnetic braking systems in baitcasting reels, helping anglers cast farther with fewer backlashes. Later came innovations like the T-Wing System (TWS), which reduced friction during the cast by allowing line to flow more freely before returning to a narrow channel during the retrieve. For bass anglers pitching jigs, burning lipless crankbaits or launching oversized swimbaits, longer, more controlled casts became an immediate advantage.

That pursuit eventually led to Daiwa’s SV, or Stress-Free Versatile, technology, which takes a more dynamic approach to controlling spool speed. Braking force is applied when spool speed is at its highest — when overrun and backlash are most likely — and then reduced as the spool slows, allowing the lure to continue its flight with less resistance.

SV BOOST pushed the concept another step forward. The system helps control the spool during the explosive beginning of a cast, then progressively releases braking force as the lure travels. The result is the balance baitcasting anglers have always chased: control without giving away casting distance.

The same engineering-first mindset led to MAGSEALED technology, which borrowed magnetic-fluid concepts from aerospace applications to better protect reel internals from water and contaminants while maintaining smooth performance. It represented one of the first truly new reel technologies in decades and demonstrated that innovation could come from well outside the fishing industry.

1976: Daiwa’s Influence Extends Well Beyond Reels

As bass fishing became increasingly technique-specific, Daiwa responded with rod technologies aimed at maximizing sensitivity without adding weight. High-density carbon construction, X45 Bias Wrap technology and Air Guide System (AGS) carbon guides all reflected the company’s pursuit of lighter, stronger and more responsive rods.

For anglers fishing deep structure with jigs, feeling subtle bites on offshore schools or presenting finesse baits with spinning tackle, every ounce removed from a rod and every vibration transmitted through the blank mattered. Daiwa recognized those needs early and built products to meet them.

2013 Tatula Type-R: Built With B.A.S.S. Anglers In Mind
Perhaps no product line better illustrates Daiwa’s commitment to American bass fishing than Tatula.

Introduced more than a decade ago, the series combined many of Daiwa’s flagship technologies into equipment priced for everyday anglers while incorporating direct feedback from touring professionals. Today, Tatula has become one of the most recognizable names in bass fishing, trusted by weekend anglers and Progressive Bassmaster Elite Series pros alike.

That relationship with competitive bass fishing extends beyond the tackle itself. For more than six years, Daiwa has served as a Supporting Sponsor of B.A.S.S. while maintaining a roster of pro anglers competing across B.A.S.S. tournament trails.
For Daiwa, those relationships provide something particularly valuable to a company built around engineering: a direct connection to the people using its products.

B.A.S.S. events bring together pro anglers, weekend fishermen, dealers, fans and others within the industry, giving Daiwa an opportunity to put its equipment in front of customers while gathering feedback from anglers who test tackle under the most demanding conditions imaginable.

It also keeps the company connected to the larger community that has helped build bass fishing. Supporting tournaments, anglers and events strengthens relationships with dealers and customers while investing in the competitive side of the sport that has helped drive tackle innovation for generations.

In that sense, Daiwa’s relationship with B.A.S.S. follows much the same philosophy as its approach to product development: Stay close to anglers, listen to what they need and use that knowledge to help move the sport forward.

Sixty years after establishing its U.S. presence, Daiwa continues to push tackle design forward while honoring the engineering philosophy that built its reputation. The company’s Limited Edition 60th Anniversary Daiwa rods and reels (spinning and baitcasting) celebrate that milestone, but they also serve as a reminder that innovation has never been a destination for Daiwa — it’s simply part of the journey.

In a sport driven by constant evolution, few companies have left fingerprints on modern bass fishing the way Daiwa has. From lightweight carbon construction and advanced braking systems to technique-specific rods and revolutionary reel designs, generations of anglers have benefited from ideas that began on an engineer’s drawing board.
And if history is any indication, the next great innovation is probably already there.

Daiwa’s first spinning reel rolled off the assembly line in 1955. Since then, the company has grown into one of the largest and most influential tackle companies in the world today. To handle sales and distribution in the United States, Daiwa Corporation first opened its doors on September 26, 1966, operating from a small facility in Culver City, California. Today, based in Foothill Ranch, California, Daiwa Corporation sells tackle throughout the United States, Canada, Central and South America. From the very beginning, Daiwa’s emphasis has been upon innovation and quality. The result is a long list of product features, design and materials that have become standards for the fishing tackle industry. Daiwa’s long-standing record of innovation has left a visible mark on the majority of tackle manufactured today and continues to advance the sport of fishing. Learn more at daiwa.us.
